prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: These, FrenchKisses, Why

outputs.L1:
I thank the spiders’ webs and the circus dancers who stain our eyes with rapid movements, authorizing our handcuffs to make no distinction between night and day, or love and hate.

No one will ever know the sum of our arduous daily separations from bed to work. These pillars actually belong to you, since I have neither counted them nor know, any more than you do, where they are or in what country they still exist. We can put all our concerns into a loaf of bread and French kisses, go to the movies, and watch the milk splashing across the screen, imitating the forest in the moonlight.

Why all the fuss about the patrons becoming feathers and discharging their ideas of nobility on the evening news? There are no lights in the theater, only soft snow falling from the balcony—the little red schoolhouse where all this began.

Actually, it was because of you that I did not attend as often as I should have. I was too embarrassed to face you across the clay-modeling tables, since I always felt that the clay in your hands was a cartoon version of my teenage years, dear slippery-fish ladies of the sleepy West.

Don’t forget: my early life will be yours, too,  
with its self-descriptions of poetic justice.  
The tiny creatures we write about can describe themselves  
in the moss we leave behind.
outputs.L2:
My gratitude goes to the cobwebs and to the acrobats whose quick gestures blur our sight, permitting our restraints to ignore every boundary—between darkness and daylight, affection and loathing.

Nobody will ever calculate the full burden of our difficult, repeated departures each day, from sleep toward labor. In truth, these columns are yours: I never numbered them, and I know no better than you where they stand, which nation contains them, or whether they remain at all.

We might tuck every worry into bread and French kisses, then visit the cinema, where milk bursts across the screen and pretends to be a moonlit forest. So why the uproar when benefactors turn into plumage and broadcast their notions of honor during the nightly news? The auditorium has no lamps. Instead, gentle snow drifts from the balcony—the small crimson schoolhouse in which everything started.

To be honest, you were the reason my attendance was poorer than it ought to have been. I felt too ashamed to sit opposite you at the tables used for shaping clay, because the material beneath your fingers always seemed like a caricature of my adolescence, my dear slick, fishlike women from the drowsy West.

Remember this as well: my beginnings will also belong to you, along with their accounts of justice made poetic. The minute beings that enter our writing are capable of telling their own stories in the moss we abandon.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by expressing gratitude for the surreal forces that dissolve familiar boundaries, blurring the distinctions between night and day, love and hate, and other apparent opposites. In this uncertain atmosphere, daily life becomes an exhausting cycle of separation: leaving the comfort of bed for work, then leaving work to return to bed. Yet the true weight of this routine remains difficult to measure or fully understand.

Against that burden, ordinary pleasures provide a kind of refuge. Bread, kisses, and movies offer simple, immediate comfort, allowing the speaker to retreat from social anxieties and from public performances of virtue or nobility. These modest experiences feel more genuine than grand ideals or outward displays of moral importance.

The speaker also turns toward a painful personal memory, recalling how embarrassment once led them to avoid someone. This recollection is connected to a deeper sense of loss: the feeling that other people had taken their youth and reshaped it into something distorted and unfamiliar. Nevertheless, the passage ends with a suggestion of endurance. Personal history, poetic justice, and even the smallest living creatures survive through the marks and traces they leave behind, ensuring that what has passed is never entirely erased.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents modern life as a disorienting mixture of routine, memory, desire, and performance. Its surreal images of work, theater, school, and intimate relationships transform familiar experiences into something strange and unstable. Work suggests repetition and alienation, while the theater introduces the sense that people are both actors and spectators in their own lives. School evokes the formative power of the past, recalling the places where identity, language, and social expectations first take shape. Images of love and intimacy offer moments of connection, but these moments remain intertwined with distance, uncertainty, and the difficulty of fully understanding another person.

Throughout the poem, memory disrupts any clear separation between past and present. Personal history does not appear as an orderly narrative; instead, it returns in fragments, associations, and unexpected images. This fragmented structure reflects the way memory actually works, bringing together experiences that may be separated by years but remain emotionally connected. The poem’s surrealism therefore serves a serious purpose: it reveals how ordinary life is shaped by impressions that cannot always be explained through conventional logic.

The poem is also deeply self-conscious about the act of artistic creation. It does not simply recount experience but repeatedly draws attention to the way experience is selected, reshaped, and preserved through language. Poetry becomes another kind of stage, one on which the speaker reconstructs work, education, love, and loss. Yet the poet’s authority remains limited. The speaker cannot claim complete ownership of these memories because they involve other people, shared institutions, inherited language, and collective forms of experience.

By the conclusion, the poem suggests that personal history is never entirely private. Individual lives are made from encounters with others, and the poems created from those lives also enter a shared cultural space. What begins as an apparently solitary reflection thus becomes a meditation on connection and survival. Even lives that seem small, repetitive, or overlooked leave traces—in memories, relationships, objects, gestures, and words. Poetry gathers these traces and gives them form, allowing ordinary existence to preserve and articulate itself beyond the moment in which it was lived.
outputs.L5:
**Why These FrenchKisses Matter**

These FrenchKisses are more than fleeting moments of romance. They carry the excitement of a first connection, the warmth of affection, and the mystery of emotions left unspoken. Why do they feel so unforgettable? Perhaps because they turn an ordinary moment into a memory that lingers long after two people part.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist prose poem about work, memory, art school, cinema, and lost intimacy, using dreamlike imagery and abrupt associative transitions.
counterfactuals.output:
At nine the office opens its mechanical eyelid. We enter carrying briefcases full of rain. Someone stamps the morning until it resembles permission; someone else staples a blue horizon to the invoice. My desk has begun to grow teeth, small ivory deadlines that click when I remember your hands.

In art school we were taught to draw the absence around a chair. Charcoal darkened our fingerprints. The plaster saints watched us fail beautifully. You slept beneath the etching press one February, your coat smelling of turpentine and snow, while I painted a red door over and over, unable to admit it was your mouth.

Then cinema: a corridor of illuminated dust.

On the screen, a woman runs beside a train that is leaving her childhood. The audience eats quietly. Horses gallop through a close-up of an eye. A match is struck; suddenly it is summer, suddenly my mother is young and arranging oranges in a bowl that has not yet broken. The projector coughs up our faces, frame by frame, but places them on strangers.

At lunch I find a beach inside the photocopier. Black waves repeat themselves. My supervisor asks for the report, and I hand him a gull. He does not notice. Outside, elevators carry the dead between floors, each holding a paper cup, each late for a meeting.

Memory has poor lighting. It splices carelessly.

You are washing paint from your wrists.  
You are asleep in the last row.  
You are saying stay, though perhaps it was the radiator.  
You are turning away, though perhaps it was the film burning.

Years later, I still clock in beneath that red door. I answer emails from abandoned museums. I file the moon under Miscellaneous. At five, the building exhales us onto the street, where every window is showing the same silent picture: two people in a kitchen, almost touching, while snow falls upward into the unfinished sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a fragmented free-verse monologue in the style of postmodern American poetry, blending spiders, circus dancers, handcuffs, bread, French kisses, and a snowy theater balcony.
counterfactuals.output:
I arrived late—  
the spiders had already stitched  
their small republic  
between the seats.

Below, circus dancers  
turned their red ankles  
through hoops of applause,  
each body a question  
the body refused to answer.

You said love.  
Or loaf.  
The theater was snowing indoors;  
white gathered along the balcony rail,  
on our coats, our eyelashes,  
the handcuffs linking my left wrist  
to your elegant mistake.

Somewhere backstage  
bread cooled on a windowsill  
that had no window.

I remember this clearly  
because memory is a liar  
with excellent diction.

We kissed—French, allegedly—  
while the orchestra folded  
its black wings.

A spider crossed your tongue.  
No, a shadow.  
No, the thin acrobat  
of what I could not say.

Below us, the dancers kept falling  
upward.

The snow entered my pockets.  
The bread broke itself.

And the handcuffs—  
bright little parentheses—  
held us inside  
an unfinished sentence

until the curtain rose  
on nothing,

and nothing  
took a bow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental poem addressed to a mysterious former classmate, recalling embarrassing encounters across clay-modeling tables and reflecting on how the past is shared.
counterfactuals.output:
**Kiln-Side, to the Classmate Whose Name I Misremember**

You—  
with the thumbprint moon  
pressed into your forehead  
by accident,

do you remember the clay room?

Four tables pushed together  
like continents ashamed  
of having once touched.

I was making a horse.  
You said, *That’s a chair.*

The horse heard you  
and became furniture.

Between us:  
a bowl collapsing inward,  
a wet gray mouth  
refusing its own shape.

I laughed too loudly.  
You dropped the wire cutter.  
Someone’s sleeve dragged through the slip.  
The teacher said,  
                    *Start again,*  
as if beginning were clean.

Years later, I still find  
that afternoon under my nails.

Your name begins, perhaps, with M—  
or with the sound a kiln makes  
when cooling:  
small ticks in the dark,  
heat becoming history.

I remember reaching across you  
for the sponge  
and knocking my unfinished face  
onto the floor.

It broke exactly  
where a face should not:

                         across the wanting  
                         to be recognized.

You looked away—kindly,  
which was worse.

But listen:

the past is not mine  
because I blush in it.

It is not yours  
because you stood there  
holding the blue apron string  
between two fingers.

We carried that room out together,  
without knowing—  
one table at each corner,

the clay horses,  
the accidental bowls,  
the ruined heads  
rattling softly on top.

Sometimes I dream you remember  
a different humiliation:

that I called you by the wrong name,  
that you called me nothing,  
that our elbows touched  
and both apologized.

Perhaps memory is only this:

two hands on the same lump,  
each insisting  
the other made the dent.

M—, or whoever you became,

somewhere our fingerprints  
still cross in fired clay—  
yours entering mine,  
mine interrupting yours—

and neither of us  
able to lift them  
without breaking  
the whole small  
awkward  
shared thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, uncanny prose poem with minimal stanza breaks, irregular capitalization, and images that blur ordinary daily life with dreams, nostalgia, and cultural critique.
counterfactuals.output:
At 6:17 the refrigerator begins reciting the names of extinct birds, softly, as if ashamed of its white electric body. I stand barefoot in the blue receipt-light, eating yesterday’s cake over the sink while the neighborhood dreams through its subscription services: every window a tiny aquarium of faces, every face learning how to desire the same impossible kitchen. Mother calls from 1998 to ask whether I have found my shoes. Her voice is full of dial-up weather, little storms of static, and behind her the old television applauds a family who has correctly guessed the price of a washing machine. NO, I say, though I am wearing the shoes; they have simply forgotten me. Outside, the bus kneels at the curb like a tired animal. We climb into its fluorescent stomach carrying coffees, passwords, private ruins. A child in a dinosaur jacket points at the moon still visible above the pharmacy and whispers, clearance.  

By noon the office plants have unionized with our shadows. The copier coughs up a photograph of my childhood bedroom: wallpaper of pale rockets, dust orbiting the lamp, my father asleep in a chair beside a newspaper announcing a future that never arrived. Someone has written PRODUCTIVITY in red across his forehead. At lunch we chew salads from transparent coffins and discuss wellness, rent, the latest war packaged between weather and sports. A notification blooms; somewhere, a stranger has remembered for me the smell of cassette tape, hot plastic, rain in the school parking lot. I click the heart because grief now requires a user response. beneath the table my knees are small again, scabbed, waiting for summer to mean something other than smoke.

Evening enters wearing my grandmother’s perfume and the security guard’s uniform. In the supermarket, oranges glow with the confidence of minor gods. The self-checkout asks if I brought my own bag, my own body, my own acceptable reason for being alive after closing. Unexpected item in the Baggage Area. It is the house we lost, reduced to the size of a loaf of bread; it is Sunday dinner, steam on the windows; it is every song the mall ceiling played while our towns were quietly sold. I press SKIP, SKIP, SKIP, but the machine keeps calling for assistance. No one comes. On the walk home, advertisements turn their enormous faces toward me, tender as dictators: Be Yourself, they command, in six available colors. Above them the stars buffer endlessly. Somewhere a lawn sprinkler ticks through the dark, watering a memory of grass. i unlock my apartment and find the day sitting on my bed, older than I left it, holding a glass of milk gone silver in the moonlight. We do not speak. The refrigerator clears its throat. Another bird disappears.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical stream-of-consciousness piece that begins by thanking unlikely things, shifts through commuting and movies, remembers a little red schoolhouse, and ends with tiny creatures describing themselves in moss.
counterfactuals.output:
Thank you, cracked teacup, for keeping the shape of thirst. Thank you, bent key that opens nothing, for your stubborn little lightning. Thank you, dust beneath the radiator, patient archivist of buttons, crumbs, one blue bead, the winter legs of spiders. Thank you, wrong number ringing at midnight, proving that somewhere a hand still reaches through the dark and hopes to be answered.

Morning arrives wearing its gray coat inside out. I join the river of commuters, each of us carrying a private weather system onto the train: drizzle behind the eyes, thunder folded into a briefcase, a pale sun sleeping in someone’s scarf. The doors close with the finality of a book, and we sway together without touching, strangers practicing the ancient balance between departure and return.

Stations pass like names whispered in sleep. A woman applies lipstick in the window’s black mirror. A boy watches tunnels flare and vanish. An advertisement promises a new face, a new language, a vacation from the self. Above ground, traffic pours its red and white sentences down the avenue, and every taxi seems to be hurrying toward the last scene of a movie I have almost remembered.

Movies: yes, the dark room, the enormous moon of the screen. Cowboys riding forever across a country made of light. A woman on a fire escape saying goodbye before the rain knows it has begun. Monsters tenderly lifting their ruined hands. Lovers meeting at clocks, bridges, airports, wars—always too late, always exactly when the music requires. We sit among strangers and borrow one another’s breathing. We believe the dead can return if the projector keeps turning. We believe a door painted on a wall might open if the actor runs toward it with sufficient grief.

And then, without warning, I am back at the little red schoolhouse beyond the sumac hill, its bell rope frayed, its windows clouded with arithmetic and breath. Chalk dust drifted through the afternoon like flour from an invisible kitchen. Our coats hung from pegs, small abandoned bodies waiting for winter. On the blackboard: oceans, capitals, the careful white skeleton of a sentence. Outside, a crow walked the fence as if inspecting our mistakes.

At recess we found worlds beneath the steps: bottle caps, mica, a marble green as deep water. We pressed our ears to the earth and claimed we heard roots drinking. Perhaps we did. Children know that silence is not empty; it is crowded with shy machinery. Beneath the schoolhouse, beetles polished their armor. Worms moved through darkness without lamps. Seeds rehearsed their green explosions.

Years went by—ticket stubs, platforms, closing credits, faces reflected and replaced—and still that red building waited somewhere behind the eyes, no larger than a matchbox, bright against the snow.

Now evening kneels in the woods. Rain loosens the bark’s old handwriting. The ground exhales. I lean close to a fallen stone, and there they are: mites, springtails, beetles no bigger than commas, gathering in the velvet shade. They do not speak aloud. They move, pause, turn, and leave their delicate declarations in moss:

we are the small keepers,  
we are the almost unseen,  
we are silver feet and seed-black eyes,  
we are here, we are here, we are here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
